When Cursor wants pi to run a tool, the exchange looks like this today:

```text
Cursor -> provider : ExecServerMessage    { id: 7, mcpArgs: { toolName: "bash", args: ... } }
         (provider hands the call to pi, pi runs it, pi sends the next request)
provider -> Cursor : ExecClientMessage    { id: 7, mcpResult: { text: "<tool output>" } }
         (provider waits for Cursor to continue generating)
```

The proposal adds two control frames, both tied to that same request id:

```text
while pi is running the tool, every ~3s:
provider -> Cursor : ExecClientControlMessage { heartbeat:    { id: 7 } }   "request 7 is still running"
after the result:
provider -> Cursor : ExecClientControlMessage { stream_close: { id: 7 } }   "nothing more is coming for request 7"
```

**Why the protocol has them.** Each Cursor request is treated as a small stream, because some requests (like streaming shell output) get several replies. `stream_close` marks the end of the replies for one request. The per-request heartbeat says it's still being worked on. These are separate from the connection-wide heartbeats the provider already sends every 5s.

**Why it might cause your stalls.** If Cursor's server sometimes waits for that end marker before it carries on
